script.opening: "This is embarrassing, doctor, but my hands and armpits just drip with sweat — even when I’m cool and calm. My palms are so wet I ruin paperwork and dread shaking hands, and my shirts are soaked. It’s been like this since school. It’s really knocking my confidence at work. Is there anything that helps?"

facts.text: Since about age 13. Palms, soles and armpits, both sides equally. Happens even when cool and relaxed, worse when nervous or warm. Never at night — "it’s fine when I’m asleep". Changes shirts at lunchtime. Will hold his palm to the camera: visibly wet.
No night sweats, no fevers, no weight loss, no lumps. No palpitations, headaches or tremor. Not all over the body. No new medicines. Not diabetic. No change in pattern recently.
If asked how much it interferes, on a scale where 1 is never noticeable and 4 is intolerable and always interferes: "Three, I’d say — barely tolerable, often interferes."
Ordinary antiperspirants only. Never tried aluminium chloride. Carries tissues and wipes his hands on his trousers.
Well. No regular medicines. No glaucoma, no bladder problems. No allergies. Not sure about family — "Mum’s hands were always clammy, now I think about it".

Works as an estate agent — shaking hands and signing contracts all day. Has turned down a promotion that involves presentations. Avoids holding hands with his new girlfriend. Anxious sometimes, "fed up", not depressed. Non-smoker, drinks 10 units a week.

Embarrassed, apologetic for "wasting your time with sweat". Relax if the doctor takes it seriously. Ask: "Does it work on hands?" and "And my armpits if the cream doesn’t work?". Happy to start with a cream.

ice.expectations: "Something that helps — I’d heard about injections."

cues: "It’s really knocking my confidence" — explore the impact on work and relationships.
"It’s fine when I’m asleep" — supports primary focal hyperhidrosis.
"I thought nothing could be done" — he needs to know there is a stepwise plan.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PRIMARY FOCAL HYPERHIDROSIS — localised, bilateral/symmetrical palm/sole/axilla/face sweating, young onset, even when not hot but sleep-sparing, often familial

Distinguishes SECONDARY hyperhidrosis and its RED FLAGS (generalised/asymmetric, night sweats, weight loss, later onset, systemic symptoms — thyroid, infection/TB, malignancy/lymphoma, menopause, diabetes, phaeo, drugs) warranting a work-up

Manages STEPWISE — first-line topical aluminium chloride with the correct technique (dry skin at bedtime, washed off in the morning), then iontophoresis (palms/soles), oral anticholinergics (oxybutynin off-label; topical glycopyrronium specialist/local formulary only), and botulinum toxin (axillae) — with practical advice and an HDSS severity score
Refers to dermatology for severe/refractory cases or specialist treatments (and considers surgery in selected severe cases), and treats any identified secondary cause
ACKNOWLEDGES the major psychosocial impact and validates it as a recognised, treatable condition (not a hygiene failing), addressing his embarrassment
Explains the stepwise options and realistic expectations, checking understanding
Explores the impact on his work, relationships and confidence and what a good outcome would look like for him, and tailors the stepwise plan to his priorities

Safety-nets and follows up: review of treatment response and escalation, investigation if any secondary red flags, referral if severe, and impact support — recognising primary focal hyperhidrosis and treating it, not dismissing it

worked.txt: "First, this is a genuine medical condition called hyperhidrosis — not you being unhygienic or ‘just sweaty’, and it’s treatable. The pattern you describe — hands and armpits since school, even when you’re cool, but fine when you’re asleep — is the common, harmless type."

"Just to be thorough — is the sweating all over your body or just these areas? Any night sweats, weight loss, or feeling generally unwell? … No, it’s focal and you’re otherwise well, which is reassuring."

"We treat it in steps. First-line is a strong aluminium-chloride antiperspirant — it can be very effective. Put it on completely dry skin at bedtime and wash it off in the morning, every night at first and then less often as it works; don’t shave just before. I’ll start you on that."

"If that’s not enough, there are good options: a treatment called iontophoresis for the hands, tablets that reduce sweating (one of them, oxybutynin, isn’t licensed for this, so we’d discuss that), creams through the specialists, and Botox injections, which work really well for the armpits. So there’s a clear path even if step one isn’t enough."
"I can hear how much this affects your confidence and work — that’s completely understandable, and it’s exactly why it’s worth treating properly rather than putting up with."

"If it stays severe despite these, I’ll refer you to dermatology for the injections or other options. Come back if it’s not improving, or if you ever develop sweating all over, night sweats or weight loss — that I’d want to look into differently."

f.learning: PRIMARY FOCAL HYPERHIDROSIS is excessive LOCALISED sweating of the PALMS, SOLES, AXILLAE and/or face, typically BILATERAL and SYMMETRICAL, with onset in childhood/adolescence, occurring even when the person is not hot but characteristically STOPPING during SLEEP, often with a family history and worsened by stress — a benign, recognised condition. Distinguish it from SECONDARY (often generalised) hyperhidrosis, whose red flags warrant a work-up: generalised or asymmetric sweating, NIGHT sweats, weight loss, later-life onset, or systemic symptoms — prompting consideration of hyperthyroidism, infection (including TB), malignancy/lymphoma, menopause, diabetes/hypoglycaemia, anxiety, phaeochromocytoma and drugs. Manage primary focal hyperhidrosis STEPWISE: first-line topical ALUMINIUM CHLORIDE hexahydrate 20% (BNF), applied to completely dry skin at bedtime and washed off in the morning, then iontophoresis (especially palms/soles), topical anticholinergics (glycopyrronium — specialist or local formulary use only), oral anticholinergics (propantheline, dose per BNF; oxybutynin off-label — weighing side-effects), and BOTULINUM TOXIN A injections (effective for severe axillary hyperhidrosis; specialist), with practical advice (absorbent clothing, sweat shields) and severity scored with the HDSS (International Hyperhidrosis Society, international; 3 or 4 = severe). Refer to dermatology for severe/refractory cases or specialist treatments, and consider surgery (endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy, NICE HTG339, formerly IPG487) in carefully selected severe upper-limb cases after other treatments, with counselling that compensatory sweating is usual and can be severe; treat any identified secondary cause. Crucially, acknowledge the major psychosocial impact (confidence, work, social life, relationships, anxiety) and validate that this is a treatable medical condition, not a hygiene failing. The skill is recognising primary focal hyperhidrosis, excluding secondary red flags, stepwise treatment, referral if severe, and addressing the impact.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BNF aluminium chloride hexahydrate monograph · [2] BNF botulinum toxin type A monograph (severe axillary hyperhidrosis, specialist use) · [3] BNF propantheline bromide and other antimuscarinic monographs · [4] NICE HTG339 (formerly IPG487): endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy for primary hyperhidrosis of the upper limb (2014) · [5] International Hyperhidrosis Society (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale) (international)
knowledge.summary: Symmetrical sweating of the palms, soles and armpits since adolescence, even when cool, but not during sleep, is primary focal hyperhidrosis. It is common, harmless and treatable, but it can hurt confidence, work and relationships. Check for the features of secondary sweating, score severity, start aluminium chloride with the right technique, and step up to iontophoresis, antimuscarinics or botulinum toxin, with dermatology referral for severe or resistant disease.

points.t: Focal, visible, excessive sweating for at least six months, typically bilateral and symmetrical, affecting palms, soles, armpits or face. It starts in childhood or adolescence, often runs in families, and stops during sleep. It is not a hygiene problem.

Generalised or one-sided sweating, night sweats, onset in later adulthood, weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, palpitations or tremor. Consider hyperthyroidism, infection including TB, lymphoma and other cancers, diabetes and hypoglycaemia, menopause, phaeochromocytoma, and drugs such as antidepressants. These need a targeted work-up; primary focal disease does not need routine tests.

The Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale grades impact from 1 (never noticeable) to 4 (intolerable, always interferes) [5]. A score of 3 or 4 means severe disease and helps decide on escalation and referral.

Aluminium chloride hexahydrate 20% applied to completely dry skin at night and washed off in the morning, building up the number of nights as tolerated, then reducing to maintenance as it works [1]. Irritation is the common problem: apply only to dry skin, reduce frequency and avoid shaving just before use.

Tap-water iontophoresis for palms and soles (usually via dermatology or physiotherapy, or a home device). Oral antimuscarinics such as propantheline for widespread or multi-site sweating; dry mouth, blurred vision and constipation limit use (BNF [3]; dose per BNF). Botulinum toxin A for severe axillary disease, given by a specialist [2]. Topical glycopyrronium cream is an option for severe axillary disease in adults when aluminium chloride and oral antimuscarinics have not worked or are unsuitable (NICE TA1175, 2026).

Refer to dermatology if topical treatment fails or disease is severe. Endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy is for severe upper-limb disease after other treatments. NICE HTG339 supports it, but patients must understand that compensatory sweating elsewhere is usual and can be severe [4].
Anxiety, social avoidance and low mood are common. Validate the burden, ask what matters most to him, and screen for social anxiety, which may need its own help.

model.text: Hello Mr Marsh, I’m Dr Singh. What can I help with today?

This is embarrassing, doctor, but my hands and armpits just drip with sweat, even when I’m cool and calm. My palms are so wet I ruin paperwork and dread shaking hands, and my shirts are soaked. It’s been like this since school. It’s really knocking my confidence at work. Is there anything that helps?

Thank you for telling me. Lots of people find this hard to bring up, and it’s a real medical problem. I’ll ask some questions, have a quick look, and then we’ll go through the treatments. Is that all right?
Yes, thanks.
Where exactly do you sweat, and is it the same on both sides?
Palms, feet and armpits. Both sides equally.
Does it happen at night? Do you ever wake up drenched?
No. It’s fine when I’m asleep. It’s the daytime.
Any weight loss, fevers, lumps in your neck or armpits, racing heart, shakiness, or feeling hot all the time?
No, none of that.
Do you take any medicines or supplements, and does anyone in your family have the same thing?
No regular medicines. I’m not sure about the family.
What have you tried so far?
Just ordinary antiperspirants.
You said it’s knocking your confidence. How does it affect your day?
I avoid shaking hands, I worry about my shirts all day, and I don’t go out as much as I used to.
On a scale where 1 is never noticeable and 4 is intolerable and always interferes, where would you put it?
Three, I’d say.
That’s a lot to carry. What did you think was going on?
I just thought I’m a sweaty person and nothing could be done.
Does it make you feel anxious or low?
Anxious sometimes. Not depressed, just fed up.
If treatment worked, what would be different for you?
model.why: Explores what a good outcome means to him

model.text: Shaking hands without thinking about it. Not ruining paperwork.
Can I look at your hands and feel your neck and armpits for glands, and check your pulse?
Sure.

Your palms are visibly wet, and there are no enlarged glands, your thyroid feels normal and your pulse is steady. This is called primary hyperhidrosis. The sweat glands are overactive in certain areas. It’s common, it often starts in the teens, it isn’t harmful, and it isn’t anything to do with hygiene. It’s treatable.
I wish I’d asked years ago.

The first step is a strong antiperspirant, aluminium chloride. The trick is to put it on completely dry skin at bedtime and wash it off in the morning. Use it every night at first, then less often once it’s working. It can sting, so don’t put it on straight after shaving.
Does it work on hands?

It works best on armpits, and can help hands and feet. If it isn’t enough for your hands, a treatment called iontophoresis, where you put your hands in water with a mild electric current, works well for palms and soles. I can refer you to dermatology for that.
And my armpits if the cream doesn’t work?

Specialists can give botulinum toxin injections, which work well for armpits and last several months. There are also tablets that reduce sweating, but they can cause a dry mouth and blurred vision, so we’d weigh that up. An operation exists for severe hand sweating, but it often causes heavy sweating elsewhere, so it’s very much a last resort.
Okay. I’ll start with the cream.
Good. In the meantime, loose cotton or moisture-wicking shirts, undershirts or sweat pads, and carrying a small towel can help at work.

Come back if you start sweating at night, all over, or on one side only, or notice weight loss, fevers or lumps, because that would need checking differently. Otherwise, let’s review in about six weeks, and I’ll refer you if the cream isn’t enough. Can you tell me the plan?
model.why: Specific red flags, review and teach-back

model.text: Cream on dry skin at night, wash off in the morning. Back in six weeks, or sooner if I get night sweats, weight loss or lumps. Then maybe iontophoresis or injections.
Spot on. And if the anxiety keeps holding you back, tell me. There’s help for that too.
model.why: Leaves the door open for psychological support

social.t: Wet paperwork and handshakes affect professional confidence. Practical tips (towel, absorbent fabrics, spare shirt) help while treatment takes effect.
Social avoidance is common. Ask directly and offer help for social anxiety if it persists.

legal.t: Most people manage without formal adjustments. If severe disease has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities, the Equality Act 2010 may apply; this is decided case by case.

professional.t: Embarrassing symptoms are often presented late. A respectful, non-judgemental approach builds trust (GMC Good medical practice).
Check the BNF and local formulary for antimuscarinic doses and cautions, and for local funding rules for botulinum toxin and iontophoresis.

community.t: Hyperhidrosis UK offers patient information and peer support.

redFlags: Palpitations, tremor or heat intolerance; onset in later adulthood

playbook.diagnosis: Primary focal hyperhidrosis (palmar, plantar and axillary), severe (HDSS 3): symmetrical, onset in adolescence, sleep-sparing, no features of a secondary cause.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This is primary hyperhidrosis. The sweat glands in your hands, feet and armpits are overactive. It’s common, it isn’t harmful and it isn’t about hygiene, and there are treatments that work.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you were just a sweaty person and nothing could be done. It’s a recognised condition and we have a clear step-by-step plan.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the impact; practical work tips; screen for and support social anxiety.
sharedPlan: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate 20% to dry skin at night, washed off in the morning (BNF)
Dermatology referral for iontophoresis (palms and soles) or botulinum toxin (axillae) if first-line fails
Antimuscarinics such as propantheline considered, dose per BNF
Sympathectomy only for severe resistant upper-limb disease after counselling (NICE HTG339)
safetyNet: Return for night sweats, generalised or one-sided sweating, weight loss, fever or lumps
Return if anxiety or mood worsens

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating the problem as trivial. The marks are for recognising a real condition, ruling out the serious look-alikes, and giving a plan that works.

items.why: Sweating that continues in sleep points to a secondary cause.

items.fail: Ordering a battery of tests for classic primary disease.
items.why: Primary focal hyperhidrosis needs no routine tests.
items.fix: Test only when red flags are present.

items.fail: Prescribing aluminium chloride without explaining technique.
items.why: Morning use on damp skin causes irritation and failure.
items.fix: Dry skin, bedtime, wash off in the morning.

items.fail: Offering surgery as a quick cure.
items.why: Compensatory sweating is usual and can be severe.
items.fix: Present it as a last resort after full counselling.

items.fail: Treating it as a hygiene issue.
items.why: It deepens the shame he already feels.
items.fix: Name it as a medical condition and acknowledge the impact.

items.why: Many people need to step up treatment.
items.fix: Review at about six weeks with clear escalation.

Looked at hands; checked lymph nodes, thyroid and pulse; no routine tests for primary focal disease; HDSS scored.
Primary focal hyperhidrosis versus secondary causes: hyperthyroidism, infection, lymphoma, diabetes, drugs, phaeochromocytoma.
Asked about night sweats, generalised or one-sided sweating, weight loss, fevers, lumps and palpitations.
Primary focal hyperhidrosis (palmar, plantar and axillary), severe (HDSS 3).
Aluminium chloride with correct technique; iontophoresis for palms and soles; botulinum toxin for axillae; antimuscarinics; sympathectomy last resort; practical advice.
Screened for social anxiety and low mood; offered further help.
Return for secondary red flags; review at about six weeks; dermatology referral if first-line fails.

social.t: Wet paperwork and handshakes affect professional confidence. Practical tips (towel, absorbent fabrics, spare shirt) help while treatment takes effect.
Social avoidance is common. Ask directly and offer help for social anxiety if it persists.

legal.t: Most people manage without formal adjustments. If severe disease has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities, the Equality Act 2010 may apply; this is decided case by case.

professional.t: Embarrassing symptoms are often presented late. A respectful, non-judgemental approach builds trust (GMC Good medical practice).
Check the BNF and local formulary for antimuscarinic doses and cautions, and for local funding rules for botulinum toxin and iontophoresis.

community.t: Hyperhidrosis UK offers patient information and peer support.

redFlags: Palpitations, tremor or heat intolerance; onset in later adulthood

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Primary focal hyperhidrosis (palmar, plantar and axillary), severe (HDSS 3): symmetrical, onset in adolescence, sleep-sparing, no features of a secondary cause.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This is primary hyperhidrosis. The sweat glands in your hands, feet and armpits are overactive. It’s common, it isn’t harmful and it isn’t about hygiene, and there are treatments that work.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought you were just a sweaty person and nothing could be done. It’s a recognised condition and we have a clear step-by-step plan.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the impact; practical work tips; screen for and support social anxiety.
sharedPlan: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate 20% to dry skin at night, washed off in the morning (BNF)
Dermatology referral for iontophoresis (palms and soles) or botulinum toxin (axillae) if first-line fails
Antimuscarinics such as propantheline considered, dose per BNF
Sympathectomy only for severe resistant upper-limb disease after counselling (NICE HTG339)
safetyNet: Return for night sweats, generalised or one-sided sweating, weight loss, fever or lumps
Return if anxiety or mood worsens

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating the problem as trivial. The marks are for recognising a real condition, ruling out the serious look-alikes, and giving a plan that works.

items.why: Sweating that continues in sleep points to a secondary cause.

items.fail: Ordering a battery of tests for classic primary disease.
items.why: Primary focal hyperhidrosis needs no routine tests.
items.fix: Test only when red flags are present.

items.fail: Prescribing aluminium chloride without explaining technique.
items.why: Morning use on damp skin causes irritation and failure.
items.fix: Dry skin, bedtime, wash off in the morning.

items.fail: Offering surgery as a quick cure.
items.why: Compensatory sweating is usual and can be severe.
items.fix: Present it as a last resort after full counselling.

items.fail: Treating it as a hygiene issue.
items.why: It deepens the shame he already feels.
items.fix: Name it as a medical condition and acknowledge the impact.

items.why: Many people need to step up treatment.
items.fix: Review at about six weeks with clear escalation.
